To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PGC‐1alpha transgenic mice crossed with SOD‐1 mutant G93a mice exhibit slower progression and less severe disease than G93a mice.

PGC‐1a transgenic mice crossed with ALS‐SOD1G93A mutant mice exhibit improved survival and motor function, as well as reduced motor neuron loss and degeneration of neuomuscular junctions in the spinal cord and diaphragm.
PGC‐1alpha transgenic mice crossed with SOD 1 mutant G93a DL mice exhibited a moderate but non significant increase in average lifespan, and a significant slowing of disease progression.

the development of new therapeutic strategies to treat ALS.
the study of the role of PGC‐1 in the pathogenesis of ALS, and the identification of novel targets for the treatment of ALS.
the study of the molecular mechanisms underlying neurodegenerative diseases, in particular amyotrophic lateral slerosis (ALS).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PGC‐1a has a beneficial effect on the progression of ALS in the mouse model, but the onset of the disease was not altered.
PGC‐1a has a significant effect on the progression of ALS, but not the onset.
PGC‐1a is beneficial for ALS patients, but it is not a panacea.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PGC-1α is protective against ALS in the G93A SOD1 mouse model.
the PGC‐α gene has a protective effect in ALS.
the PGC‐ 1α gene is a potential therapeutic target for ALS.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PGC-1α has a neuroprotective role in the SOD1G93A ALS mouse model and may be useful as a therapeutic agent in human ALS.
PGC-1α has beneficial effects in ALS.
